fetched_contents.text: On Evaluation of 6D Object Pose Estimation Tomas Hodan, Jiri Matas, Stepan Obdrzalek Center for Machine Perception, Czech Technical University in Prague Abstract. A pose of a rigid object has 6 degrees of freedom and its full knowledge is required in many robotic and scene understanding appli- cations. Evaluation of 6D object pose estimates is not straightforward. Object pose may be ambiguous due to object symmetries and occlu- sions, i.e. there can be multiple object poses that are indistinguishable in the given image and should be therefore treated as equivalent. The paper defines 6D object pose estimation problems, proposes an evalu- ation methodology and introduces three new pose error functions that deal with pose ambiguity. The new error functions are compared with functions commonly used in the literature and shown to remove cer- tain types of non-intuitive outcomes. Evaluation tools are provided at: https : //github.com/thodan/obj pose eval 1 Introduction Object localization and detection are among the core problems of computer vision. Traditional methods work with 2D images and typically describe pose of the detected object by a bounding box, which encodes 2D translation and scale [1,2]. There is no information about the object orientation and only a rough notion of the object distance. A pose of a rigid object has 6 degrees of freedom, 3 in translation and 3 in rotation, and its full knowledge is required in many robotic and scene understanding applications. Although methods trying to extract a richer pose description from 2D images exist [3,4], the task can be simplified if depth images are used as additional input data. RGB-D - aligned color and depth - images which concurrently capture appearance and geometry of the scene can be obtained by e.g. Kinect-like sensors that are common in robotic applications. Evaluation of 6D object pose estimates is not straightforward. Object pose can be ambiguous due to object symmetries and occlusions, i.e. there can be multiple object poses that are indistinguishable in the given image and should be therefore treated as equivalent (Fig. 1). This issue has been out of focus in the work on 6D object pose estimation. In evaluation of pose estimates described by 2D bounding boxes, the indistinguishable poses are treated as equivalent implicitly since all are described by the same bounding box. 2 Hodan, Matas, Obdrzalek (a) (b) (c) (d) (e) Fig. 1. Different poses of the cup (a-b) cannot be distinguished if the handle is not visible due to self-occlusion (c). Pose of the pen (d) is ambiguous if its discriminative ends are occluded by another objects (e). The main contribution of this paper are three new functions to measure error of an estimated 6D object pose w.r.t. the ground truth 6D object pose. All three are invariant under pose ambiguity, i.e. they treat the indistinguishable poses as approximately equivalent. The Visible Surface Discrepancy (eVSD ) measures misalignment over the visible surface of the object model and is thus inherently invariant under pose ambiguity. The Average and the Maximum Corresponding Point Distance (eACPD , eMCPD ) measure misalignment over the entire model surface when considering all indistinguishable poses, which are assumed known. First, at training time, it is provided with a training set T = {T1 , T2 , . . . , Tn } for a set of rigid objects represented by identifiers O = {1, 2, . . . , n}. The training data Ti may have different forms, e.g. a 3D object model or a set of RGB or RGB-D images, where each image shows one object instance in a known 6D pose. Second, at test time, it is provided with a single test RGB or RGB-D image I, which might be accompanied with information about objects that are visible in the image. The goal is to estimate a single 6D pose for each visible object instance. fetched_contents.text: BOP: Benchmark for 6D Object Pose Estimation HOT3D Banerjee et al.: Introducing HOT3D: An Egocentric Dataset for 3D Hand and Object Tracking, paper, project website, license agreement. HOT3D is a dataset for egocentric hand and object tracking in 3D. The dataset offers multi-view, RGB/monochrome, fisheye image streams showing 19 subjects interacting with 33 diverse rigid objects. The dataset also offers comprehensive ground-truth annotations including 3D poses of objects, hands, and cameras, and 3D models of hands and objects. In addition to simple pick-up/observe/put-down actions, HOT3D contains scenarios resembling typical actions in a kitchen, office, and living room environment. The dataset is recorded by two head-mounted devices from Meta: Project Aria, a research prototype of light-weight AR/AI glasses, and Quest 3, a production VR headset sold in millions of units. Ground-truth poses were obtained by a professional motion-capture system using small optical markers attached to hands and objects. Hand annotations are provided in the UmeTrack and MANO formats and objects are represented by 3D meshes with PBR materials obtained by an in-house scanner. Recordings from Aria also include the eye gaze signal and scene point clouds. In BOP, we use HOT3D-Clips, which is a curated subset of HOT3D. Each clip has 150 frames (5 seconds) which are all annotated with ground-truth poses of all modeled objects and hands and which passed visual inspection. There are 4117 clips in total, 2969 clips extracted from the training split and 1148 from the test split of HOT3D. The HOT3D-Clips subset is also used in the Multiview Egocentric Hand Tracking Challenge. Ground-truth object annotations are publicly available for training images, and also for the first frames of dynamic object onboarding sequences and all frames of static object onboarding sequences (as defined in BOP Challenge 2024). See the HOT3D whitepaper for details and the HOT3D toolkit for documentation of data format and for Python utilities (loading, undistorting fisheye images, rendering using fisheye cameras, etc.). Another useful operation for working with fisheye images is perspective cropping, which produces a locally undistorted object crop that is a suitable input for an object pose estimation stage (see Sec. 3.3 of the FoundPose paper). Code for perspective cropping is available in the FoundPose repository. HOT3D-Clips are distributed in a Webdataset-based format which can be converted to the BOP-scenewise format with a script from Anas Goudas. Anas also prepared a scripts to convert HOT3D object models (GLB, in meters) to the PLY format expected by the BOP toolkit (PLY, in millimeters). We also provide visualizations of ground-truth annotations for clips and for onboarding sequences: static (Quest 3), dynamic (Quest 3), static (Aria), dynamic (Aria).

fetched_contents.text: BOP-D: Revisiting 6D Pose Estimation Benchmarks for Better Evaluation under Visual Ambiguities Boris Meden1 Asma Brazi1,2 Steve Bourgeois1 Fabrice Mayran de Chamisso1 Vincent Lepetit2 1Université Paris-Saclay, CEA, List 2LIGM, Ecole des Ponts boris.meden@cea.fr Abstract Currently, 6D pose estimation methods are benchmarked on datasets that consider, for their ground truth annotations, visual ambiguities as only related to global object symmetries. However, as previously observed [26], visual ambiguities can also happen depending on the viewpoint or the presence of occluding objects, when disambiguating parts become hidden. The visual ambiguities are therefore actually different across images. We thus first propose an automatic method to re-annotate those datasets with a 6D pose distribution specific to each image, taking into account the visibility of the object surface in the image to correctly determine the visual ambiguities. Given this improved ground truth, we re-evaluate the state-of-the-art methods and show this greatly modify the ranking of these methods. Our annotations also allow us to benchmark recent methods able to estimate a pose distribution on real images for the first time. We will make our annotations for the T-LESS dataset and our code publicly available. 1 Introduction Visual 6D pose estimation of an object consists in determining the 3D position and orientation of this object with respect to the camera that explain the observed image. It is a key task in many application domains, such as robotics (e.g. grasping or manipulation), augmented reality, industrial quality control, etc. In such contexts, datasets of images with pose ground-truths are of primary importance, since they can be used to train learning based methods, but first and foremost to benchmark the performances of proposed approaches. The annotation accuracy of reference benchmarks, such as BOP [39] for 6D pose estimation, is thus crucial since it influences the research directions. However, annotating images of objects with their 6D poses is a complex task. This is especially true when considered objects include symmetrical parts. Indeed, as illustrated in Figure 1, an image does not necessarily correspond to a single pose solution depending on the viewpoint and occlusions. While symmetrical objects naturally imply multiple solutions, non-symmetrical objects can also yield multiple solutions in case of partial occlusions. Current reference benchmarks [39] ignore these occlusion-induced symmetries, resulting in an imperfect evaluation of the methods. As we will show, considering better ground truth distributions results in a significant change of ranking of current pose estimation methods. In this paper, we first propose a method that automatically estimates pose distributions for images that take into account the ambiguities due to the object symmetries but also to the partial occlusions. Our method exploits the current annotations as a starting point, the ground truth visibility masks of the objects, and their 3D models. While we demonstrate it on T-LESS, our method is fully automatic and can be applied to other datasets. We also re-evaluate classical metrics with these annotations to evaluate the performance of pose estimation methods that return a single pose estimate per image. This yields a strongly modified ranking of current challenger methods. Moreover, we also consider the few methods that already predict multi-modal pose distributions [7, 17]. Because of the absence of proper annotations, these methods have been evaluated quantitatively only on synthetic images and only qualitatively on real images. Thanks to our annotations, we are able to provide their first evaluation on real data. In summary, our contributions are the following: 1. 1. A novel automatic method computing a multi-modal 6D pose distributions ground truth from a unique ground truth pose and a proposal set of object symmetries; 2. 2. A comprehensive re-evaluation of 6-DOF single pose estimation methods related to the re-annotation of the T-LESS [11] ground-truth; 3. 3. A new evaluation framework of 6-DOF pose distribution estimation methods, which makes it the first multi-modal pose distribution benchmarking on real data. Our annotations and code will be made public. 2 Related Work Object 6D pose estimation aims at determining an object pose that best explains the camera observation. While the solution is unique when the object is non-symmetrical and not occluded, multiple equivalent possible solutions arise when the object is symmetrical or when the occlusions prevent the observation of symmetry-breaking elements. While the state of the art mostly focused on estimating a single pose [4, 35, 13, 21, 38, 41, 6, 37], some recent works focus on estimating the complete set of solutions [26, 33, 30, 20, 27, 16, 7, 17]. As we argue below, to properly evaluate the performance of a method, ground truth annotations including the complete set of solutions for each test image, and metrics that take into account the multiplicity of the solutions, are required, even for methods that returns a single pose per image. Datasets and 6D pose annotation. Various techniques have been introduced to annotate image datasets with their 6D poses. For synthetic datasets [2, 40], the ground truth pose is directly available, while, for real datasets, this pose is usually determined with the help of user interaction [5, 12, 3], markers [8, 9, 1], or a robotic arm [42, 28], and refined with ICP in the case of an RGB-D camera [5, 12, 42, 28]. However, such annotations only provide a single pose solution while multiple may exist. For fully symmetric objects, the solutions are always related with the same set of rigid transforms, independently of the viewpoint or the occlusions. ## Core metrics used in 6D object pose estimation

The most commonly reported metrics in 6D object pose estimation literature are **translation error**, **rotation error**, **reprojection error**, **corresponding point distance**, and **symmetry-aware variants** such as those explicitly designed to handle pose ambiguity. The literature also commonly reports **combined rotation-and-translation metrics** such as MRTE (Multi Rotation Translation Error) [N1-F1], which combine scaled rotation and translation errors into a single pose score.

### Most commonly reported metrics

The most commonly reported metrics are:

1. **Translation error** — directly measures how far the estimated 3D position deviates from the ground truth position.
2. **Rotation error** — measures how different the estimated orientation is from the ground truth orientation, often expressed as an angular distance or using rotation averaging.
3. **Reprojection error** — measures how well the projected model points match the observed image features, and is especially tied to the assumption that the camera/viewpoint is known and the object surface is visible [N1-R3][N1-F1].
4. **Corresponding point distance** — measures the geometric mismatch between the model and the image, often over the object surface, and is used both as an absolute error and as an ambiguity-aware variant [N1-F1].
5. **Symmetry-aware or ambiguity-aware metrics** — newer metrics that explicitly account for multiple equivalent poses that are indistinguishable in the image [N1-F1][N6-F3].

### How each metric quantifies pose error in 6D space

- **Translation error** quantifies the 3D position mismatch between the estimated and ground-truth pose.
- **Rotation error** quantifies the angular mismatch between the estimated and ground-truth orientation, often by computing the angle between rotation matrices or using rotation averaging [N1-F1].
- **Reprojection error** quantifies the geometric mismatch by projecting the ground-truth model into the image using the estimated pose and comparing it to observed features; this depends strongly on the camera model and viewpoint assumptions [N1-R3][N1-F1].
- **Corresponding point distance** quantifies the mismatch between the object model and the observed image, either over the visible surface or across the entire model surface, and is used to assess overall alignment [N1-F1].
- **MRTE** combines scaled rotation and translation errors into a single metric, treating them as separate components rather than conflating them into a single distance [N1-F1].

### Rotation-only, translation-only, or combined metrics

- **Rotation-only metrics** are used when the main interest is orientation accuracy; examples include angular rotation error and rotation averaging approaches.
- **Translation-only metrics** are used when the main interest is position accuracy.
- **Combined metrics** are used when both rotation and translation errors matter equally, such as MRTE [N1-F1].

### How reprojection or geometric error relates to camera/viewpoint assumptions

Reprojection error and geometric error are closely tied to the camera/viewpoint assumptions in the dataset and evaluation protocol. Reprojection error assumes that the camera model is known, that the observed image features are reliably matched to the model, and that the viewpoint provides sufficient information to project the 3D object into the image [N1-R3][N1-F1]. Similarly, geometric error can depend on whether the evaluation considers visible surfaces, full surface alignment, or viewpoint-dependent ambiguities [N1-F1]. In contrast, metrics that assume a canonical viewpoint or fixed camera geometry can be less robust when objects are occluded or symmetric, because the same pose may appear differently from different viewpoints [N6-F3].

### Benchmark and task context

The evidence also points to **dataset-specific evaluation protocols** such as BOP and related benchmarks, which are used to report these metrics and often include multiple object categories and diverse object shapes [N4-F2]. Because object shape and category affect how clearly the pose can be distinguished, different benchmarks may emphasize different metrics or combinations of metrics [N4-F2]. Overall, the literature indicates that reprojection and geometric metrics remain widely used because they provide a direct measure of how well the estimated pose explains the observed image [N1-R3][N1-F1].

## How symmetry affects metric behavior

### What makes an object symmetric in the context of pose estimation

In pose estimation, an object is symmetric if it has multiple rigid transformations that leave the object visually indistinguishable in a given image. Symmetry can be **global** (e.g., rotational or reflective symmetry of the entire object) or **viewpoint-dependent** (e.g., partial occlusions hide symmetry-breaking features) [N6-F3]. For symmetric objects, the same object can appear in many different 6D poses, even though the actual object shape is the same [N6-F3].

### Why symmetric objects can cause ambiguity or inflated error

Symmetric objects can cause ambiguity because different poses may look identical in the image, so a pose estimator may return an estimate that is visually correct but geometrically incorrect [N1-F1][N6-F3]. This can inflate error metrics if the metric treats all equivalent poses as equally wrong, rather than grouping them as essentially the same pose [N6-F3]. For example, a rotation-only metric may report a large angular error even though the object looks the same in the image, and a reprojection metric may report a large error if the wrong symmetric pose is chosen despite matching the visible surface [N1-F1][N6-F3].

### How metrics can be adjusted or interpreted differently for symmetric objects

Metrics can be adjusted or interpreted differently for symmetric objects by:

- **Treating equivalent poses as approximately equivalent**, rather than as distinct errors [N1-F1].
- **Using ambiguity-aware metrics** such as Visible Surface Discrepancy (eVSD), Average Corresponding Point Distance (eACPD), and Maximum Corresponding Point Distance (eMCPD), which are designed to be invariant or less sensitive to ambiguity [N1-F1].
- **Considering visibility masks and object models** to determine which symmetric solutions are actually visible and which are hidden [N6-F3].
- **Reporting distribution-aware or multi-modal ground truth** rather than a single pose, which changes how error is measured and interpreted [N6-F3].

### How symmetry-aware methods change the evaluation or pose representation

Symmetry-aware methods change evaluation and pose representation in several ways:

1. **Pose representation**: They often represent poses in a **symmetry-resolved or canonical form** to eliminate redundant equivalent solutions [N5-R1].
2. **Evaluation**: They shift from evaluating single-pose estimates to evaluating whether the estimate belongs to the correct ambiguity class, or whether the method can identify the correct symmetric solution [N6-F3].
3. **Metric design**: They may use **symmetry-aware loss functions** or matching losses to supervise the estimator during training [N2-R4].
4. **Benchmarking**: They may require **multi-modal ground truth distributions** instead of a single ground-truth pose, which changes how performance is measured and compared [N6-F3].

The evidence also shows that symmetry-aware methods are explicitly studied in correspondence-based pose estimation and related object-pose tasks, indicating that symmetry is a major practical concern rather than a minor corner case [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R5].

## Methodological differences across datasets and tasks

### Dataset-specific evaluation protocols and their assumptions

The evidence points to several dataset-specific evaluation protocols, including:

- **BOP** and related benchmarks, which are central to 6D object pose estimation and provide ground-truth annotations for multiple object categories [N4-F2].
- **T-LESS** and other real-world datasets, which are used to evaluate single-pose estimation methods and have been re-annotated to account for visual ambiguities [N6-F3].
- **HOT3D-Clips**, which are used in BOP and provide annotated 3D poses for multiple objects in egocentric multi-view sequences [N4-F2].

Each of these datasets has its own assumptions. BOP assumes that ground-truth annotations should reflect visual ambiguities and that methods should be benchmarked under those conditions [N6-F3]. HOT3D-Clips assumes multi-view, RGB/monochrome, and fisheye imaging, with annotations for 3D poses of objects, hands, and cameras [N4-F2]. T-LESS is used to evaluate methods that return a single pose estimate per image, and its reannotation accounts for symmetries and partial occlusions [N6-F3].

### How object shape and category affect metric choice

Object shape and category affect metric choice because symmetric objects and objects with occlusions may have multiple visually indistinguishable poses, while non-symmetric objects may have a more unique solution [N6-F3]. For symmetric objects, metrics that treat equivalent poses as approximately equivalent are more informative than simple distance-based metrics [N1-F1]. For objects with occlusions, the visibility of disambiguating features can change which symmetric solutions are possible, making the evaluation task more complex [N6-F3]. Because of this, the literature emphasizes that object shape and category should influence how ambiguity is handled in evaluation [N6-F3].

### What papers explicitly address symmetry in their evaluation

Several papers explicitly address symmetry in their evaluation:

- **BOP-D** argues that current benchmarks treat visual ambiguities as only related to global object symmetries, but that ambiguity can also arise from viewpoint and occlusions, and that this changes the evaluation ranking of methods [N6-F3].
- **Hodan et al.** explicitly defines ambiguity-aware error functions and argues that symmetric objects and occlusions can make multiple poses indistinguishable in the image [N1-F1].
- **Symmetry-aware correspondence-based methods** are explicitly studied to investigate the impact of object symmetries and the performance of symmetry-aware methods [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R5].
- **Symmetry-sensitive pose estimation** methods are developed specifically for objects with rotational symmetry and use symmetry-aware pose representations [N5-R1][N5-R3].

### How benchmark protocols handle ambiguity or multiple plausible poses

Benchmark protocols handle ambiguity and multiple plausible poses in several ways:

- **Ambiguity-aware metrics**: Hodan et al. propose metrics such as eVSD, eACPD, and eMCPD that are designed to be invariant under or less sensitive to ambiguity [N1-F1].
- **Distribution-aware ground truth**: BOP-D and related work argue that ambiguity should be captured in a **pose distribution** per image, rather than in a single pose [N6-F3].
- **Multi-modal evaluation**: The literature now considers both single-pose methods and multi-modal pose distribution methods, with separate evaluation protocols for each [N6-F3].
- **Visibility-based reannotation**: In practice, ambiguity is handled by using visibility masks, object models, and existing annotations to compute plausible symmetric solutions [N6-F3].

Overall, the evidence suggests that benchmark protocols have moved from simple single-pose evaluation to more nuanced protocols that account for symmetry, occlusions, and multiple plausible poses [N1-F1][N6-F3].

## Historical and practical trends in metric design

### How metrics have evolved from simple distance-based error to distribution-aware error

The evolution of 6D pose estimation metrics is clear in the evidence: early work used simple distance-based errors such as translation error and rotation error, while more recent work introduced **ambiguity-aware** and **distribution-aware** metrics [N1-F1][N6-F3]. Hodan et al. explicitly notes that prior work treated ambiguous poses as equivalent implicitly, while their paper proposes new error functions that remove non-intuitive outcomes and are invariant under ambiguity [N1-F1]. BOP-D then argues that current benchmarks should not only account for global symmetries but also viewpoint and occlusion-induced ambiguities, and that this should be captured in a **pose distribution per image** [N6-F3]. This marks a shift from single-pose evaluation to multi-modal or distribution-aware evaluation.

### Why reprojection or voting-based metrics are still widely used

Reprojection and voting-based metrics remain widely used because they provide a **direct geometric link** between the estimated pose and the observed image. Reprojection error measures how well the model matches the image under the estimated pose, which makes it highly relevant for camera-based pose estimation [N1-R3][N1-F1]. Voting-based methods, such as Pixel-wise Voting Network and EfficientPose, are also widely used because they aggregate geometric cues from the image and provide a compact pose estimate that can be easily evaluated [N6-R5]. These metrics remain popular because they are intuitive, relatively robust to noise, and aligned with the visual interpretation of pose estimation [N1-R3][N6-R5].

### How model-free and model-based approaches influence metric choice

Model-free and model-based approaches influence metric choice in different ways:

- **Model-based approaches** often rely on known object models and can use geometric metrics such as reprojection error, corresponding point distance, and ambiguity-aware error functions [N1-R3][N1-F1][N6-F3]. These approaches can also use symmetry-aware representations and loss functions [N5-R1][N5-R4].
- **Model-free approaches** such as Any6D rely on fewer assumptions about object geometry and are often evaluated with metrics that are robust to novel or unseen objects [N3-R2]. They may still use reprojection or geometric error, but the presence of a learned model can change how those errors are interpreted and optimized.

The evidence also shows that symmetry-aware methods are increasingly used across both model-based and model-free settings, indicating that the choice of metric is tied to the method’s assumptions and capabilities [N5-R1][N5-R4][N6-F3].

### What limitations persist in current evaluation practices

Despite progress, several limitations persist in current evaluation practices:

1. **Single-pose evaluation remains dominant**, even though symmetric objects and occlusions can produce multiple visually indistinguishable poses [N6-F3].
2. **Ambiguity is often undercounted or ignored**, because many benchmarks still assume a single ground-truth pose rather than a distribution of plausible poses [N6-F3].
3. **Metrics can be misleading for symmetric objects**, because a large error may reflect ambiguity rather than a true pose failure [N1-F1][N6-F3].
4. **Distribution-aware evaluation is still emerging**, and many methods are only evaluated on synthetic images or qualitatively on real data [N6-F3].
5. **Evaluation protocols vary across datasets**, making comparisons difficult and requiring careful attention to assumptions such as camera geometry, visibility, and object category [N4-F2][N6-F3].

Overall, the historical trend is toward richer, ambiguity-aware, and distribution-aware evaluation, but practical limitations remain in how these ideas are implemented and benchmarked [N1-F1][N6-F3].

## Core metrics used in 6D object pose estimation

The most commonly reported metrics in 6D object pose estimation literature are **translation error**, **rotation error**, **reprojection error**, **corresponding point distance**, and **symmetry-aware variants** such as those explicitly designed to handle pose ambiguity. The literature also commonly reports **combined rotation-and-translation metrics** such as MRTE (Multi Rotation Translation Error) [N1-F1], which combine scaled rotation and translation errors into a single pose score.

### Most commonly reported metrics

The most commonly reported metrics are:

1. **Translation error** — directly measures how far the estimated 3D position deviates from the ground truth position.
2. **Rotation error** — measures how different the estimated orientation is from the ground truth orientation, often expressed as an angular distance or using rotation averaging.
3. **Reprojection error** — measures how well the projected model points match the observed image features, and is especially tied to the assumption that the camera/viewpoint is known and the object surface is visible [N1-R3][N1-F1].
4. **Corresponding point distance** — measures the geometric mismatch between the model and the image, often over the object surface, and is used both as an absolute error and as an ambiguity-aware variant [N1-F1].
5. **Symmetry-aware or ambiguity-aware metrics** — newer metrics that explicitly account for multiple equivalent poses that are indistinguishable in the image [N1-F1][N6-F3].

### How each metric quantifies pose error in 6D space

- **Translation error** quantifies the 3D position mismatch between the estimated and ground-truth pose.
- **Rotation error** quantifies the angular mismatch between the estimated and ground-truth orientation, often by computing the angle between rotation matrices or using rotation averaging [N1-F1].
- **Reprojection error** quantifies the geometric mismatch by projecting the ground-truth model into the image using the estimated pose and comparing it to observed features; this depends strongly on the camera model and viewpoint assumptions [N1-R3][N1-F1].
- **Corresponding point distance** quantifies the mismatch between the object model and the observed image, either over the visible surface or across the entire model surface, and is used to assess overall alignment [N1-F1].
- **MRTE** combines scaled rotation and translation errors into a single metric, treating them as separate components rather than conflating them into a single distance [N1-F1].

### Rotation-only, translation-only, or combined metrics

- **Rotation-only metrics** are used when the main interest is orientation accuracy; examples include angular rotation error and rotation averaging approaches.
- **Translation-only metrics** are used when the main interest is position accuracy.
- **Combined metrics** are used when both rotation and translation errors matter equally, such as MRTE [N1-F1].

### How reprojection or geometric error relates to camera/viewpoint assumptions

Reprojection error and geometric error are closely tied to the camera/viewpoint assumptions in the dataset and evaluation protocol. Reprojection error assumes that the camera model is known, that the observed image features are reliably matched to the model, and that the viewpoint provides sufficient information to project the 3D object into the image [N1-R3][N1-F1]. Similarly, geometric error can depend on whether the evaluation considers visible surfaces, full surface alignment, or viewpoint-dependent ambiguities [N1-F1]. In contrast, metrics that assume a canonical viewpoint or fixed camera geometry can be less robust when objects are occluded or symmetric, because the same pose may appear differently from different viewpoints [N6-F3].

### Benchmark and task context

The evidence also points to **dataset-specific evaluation protocols** such as BOP and related benchmarks, which are used to report these metrics and often include multiple object categories and diverse object shapes [N4-F2]. Because object shape and category affect how clearly the pose can be distinguished, different benchmarks may emphasize different metrics or combinations of metrics [N4-F2]. Overall, the literature indicates that reprojection and geometric metrics remain widely used because they provide a direct measure of how well the estimated pose explains the observed image [N1-R3][N1-F1].

## How symmetry affects metric behavior

### What makes an object symmetric in the context of pose estimation

In pose estimation, an object is symmetric if it has multiple rigid transformations that leave the object visually indistinguishable in a given image. Symmetry can be **global** (e.g., rotational or reflective symmetry of the entire object) or **viewpoint-dependent** (e.g., partial occlusions hide symmetry-breaking features) [N6-F3]. For symmetric objects, the same object can appear in many different 6D poses, even though the actual object shape is the same [N6-F3].

### Why symmetric objects can cause ambiguity or inflated error

Symmetric objects can cause ambiguity because different poses may look identical in the image, so a pose estimator may return an estimate that is visually correct but geometrically incorrect [N1-F1][N6-F3]. This can inflate error metrics if the metric treats all equivalent poses as equally wrong, rather than grouping them as essentially the same pose [N6-F3]. For example, a rotation-only metric may report a large angular error even though the object looks the same in the image, and a reprojection metric may report a large error if the wrong symmetric pose is chosen despite matching the visible surface [N1-F1][N6-F3].

### How metrics can be adjusted or interpreted differently for symmetric objects

Metrics can be adjusted or interpreted differently for symmetric objects by:

- **Treating equivalent poses as approximately equivalent**, rather than as distinct errors [N1-F1].
- **Using ambiguity-aware metrics** such as Visible Surface Discrepancy (eVSD), Average Corresponding Point Distance (eACPD), and Maximum Corresponding Point Distance (eMCPD), which are designed to be invariant or less sensitive to ambiguity [N1-F1].
- **Considering visibility masks and object models** to determine which symmetric solutions are actually visible and which are hidden [N6-F3].
- **Reporting distribution-aware or multi-modal ground truth** rather than a single pose, which changes how error is measured and interpreted [N6-F3].

### How symmetry-aware methods change the evaluation or pose representation

Symmetry-aware methods change evaluation and pose representation in several ways:

1. **Pose representation**: They often represent poses in a **symmetry-resolved or canonical form** to eliminate redundant equivalent solutions [N5-R1].
2. **Evaluation**: They shift from evaluating single-pose estimates to evaluating whether the estimate belongs to the correct ambiguity class, or whether the method can identify the correct symmetric solution [N6-F3].
3. **Metric design**: They may use **symmetry-aware loss functions** or matching losses to supervise the estimator during training [N2-R4].
4. **Benchmarking**: They may require **multi-modal ground truth distributions** instead of a single ground-truth pose, which changes how performance is measured and compared [N6-F3].

The evidence also shows that symmetry-aware methods are explicitly studied in correspondence-based pose estimation and related object-pose tasks, indicating that symmetry is a major practical concern rather than a minor corner case [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R5].
